screens.title: Data Management in Multi-Service Architectures
screens.narratorSegment: In this chapter we explore how data management changes when you move from a single monolithic database to an ecosystem of small, independently deployable services. You will learn why each microservice should own its data store, how polyglot persistence lets you pick the best database type for each service, and how to design for consistency when updates span services. We’ll cover concrete AWS options — managed relational databases for transactional workloads, DynamoDB for high-scale key-value workloads, caches for low-latency reads, graph stores for relationship-rich data, and time-series engines for sensor or metric streams. You will see patterns for consistency such as eventual consistency and the Saga pattern, and practical mitigations like compensating transactions, idempotency, and correlation IDs to trace and debug cross-service flows. A short enrollment example ties these ideas together: an enrollment service using DynamoDB, a course catalog in RDS, and a payments service in RDS that coordinate via events. By the end, you should be able to choose appropriate AWS services, design a Saga for a multi-step business transaction, and apply caching and replication to improve performance while avoiding common mistakes like sharing a single database across services. Consider how your current systems would change if each team owned its own datastore: what constraints and freedoms would that create?

screens.title: Database per Service & Data Ownership
screens.narratorSegment: Database per service is a simple but powerful idea: every microservice owns its data and exposes it only through its A P I. This ownership reduces coupling between services because schema changes, migrations, and performance tuning belong to the single responsible team. A concrete example: an Order service owns orders and transactional logic in a relational store, while a Recommendation service owns a graph or document store. A common misconception is assuming a shared database simplifies coordination. While sharing can make joins across domains easy, it creates a tight coupling that prevents independent deployment, can introduce contention, and makes ownership unclear. In practice, ownership encourages clear A P I contracts and forces teams to design explicit data exchange patterns, usually through events or service APIs. The downside is that joins across services are no longer immediate; you design denormalization, A P I composition, or asynchronous synchronization instead. Key takeaway: embrace ownership to reduce blast radius, but plan for how data will be shared via events or well-defined A P I calls. Question to reflect on: which entities in your system benefit most from independent ownership and why?

Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Database per Service
Claim
Each microservice owns its database to preserve loose coupling and independent evolution.
Benefit
Independent deployments, scoped schema changes, clear ownership.
Misconception
Shared databases simplify joins — true — but they increase coupling and deployment risk.
Key Takeaway

Adopt database-per-service to isolate changes and failures; accept explicit data sharing as part of the design.

Teaching Visual — Ownership Scenarios
Order Service (Relational)
Uses relational model for transactions, foreign keys, and ACID guarantees for payments and order state.
Recommendation Service (Graph)
Uses graph patterns for relationships and fast traversal when building recommendations.
Enrollment Service (NoSQL)
Stores high-volume writes and simple lookups with DynamoDB for throughput.
Cache Layer
ElastiCache for frequently read but mutable data to reduce load on primary stores.
Common mistake
Putting all services on one relational DB for convenience leads to scaling and ownership problems.
Reflect
If you split a monolith today, which tables should each team own first?

screens.title: Choosing AWS Datastores
screens.narratorSegment: Choosing the right AWS datastore should start from the access pattern and consistency requirements. Amazon RDS and Aurora are suited for workloads needing strong transactional consistency, complex joins, and ACID semantics — for example, a payments ledger or order management. DynamoDB is ideal when you need massive scale, low-latency key-value or document access such as user sessions or a high-write enrollment log. ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) is a purpose-built cache for frequently read, mutable data where in-memory latency matters more than durable storage, such as session stores or product detail caching. Neptune fits workloads where relationships are first-class, like recommendations or fraud detection. DocumentDB is useful for flexible schema document models compatible with MongoDB patterns. Timestream is optimized for time-series use cases like IoT sensor streams or application metrics. A frequent error is selecting a relational database for every workload by habit. Instead, base your choice on query patterns, required latency, expected scale, and consistency needs. Example: an Enrollment service that must accept high-volume writes with occasional reads is a good DynamoDB candidate, while the Course catalog with complex joins and normalized relations fits Aurora. Consider replication and cache strategies as part of your datastore decision, not an afterthought. Which trade-offs are acceptable for your service: eventual consistency or immediate transactional guarantees?

keyIdea.text: Pick databases by access pattern: relational for transactions, DynamoDB for scale, ElastiCache for low-latency reads, Neptune/DocumentDB/Timestream for specialized models.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › AWS Datastores
Service vs Pattern Table
Amazon RDS / Aurora
Strong consistency, ACID, complex joins, transactional workloads.
Amazon DynamoDB
Key-value / document, massive scale, low-latency, serverless.
Amazon ElastiCache
In-memory caching for low-latency reads; Redis or Memcached.
Amazon Neptune
Graph database for relationship-heavy queries like recommendations.
Amazon DocumentDB
MongoDB-compatible document workloads with flexible schemas.
Amazon Timestream
Time-series data for IoT and metrics with specific query optimizations.
Concrete example
Enrollment Service: high write throughput and occasional reads → DynamoDB. Course Catalog: normalized data and complex queries → Aurora. Session store: ephemeral, low-latency access → ElastiCache.
Mistake to avoid
Defaulting every service to a relational database creates scaling and deployment bottlenecks.
Key Takeaway

Match datastore capabilities to workload needs: scale, latency, schema flexibility, and consistency guarantees.

screens.title: Eventual Consistency Explained
screens.narratorSegment: Eventual consistency means that if no new updates occur, all replicas of a data item will converge to the latest value over time. This model contrasts with strong consistency, where every read reflects the latest write immediately. Eventual consistency is acceptable for many user experiences where a slight delay is tolerable — for instance, updating a user profile photo across services or reflecting an enrollment status that moves from PENDING to CONFIRMED. A misconception is that eventual consistency is unreliable; in reality, it is a deliberate trade-off to gain availability and latency. Design patterns that embrace eventual consistency include optimistic updates, user-facing pending states, and conflict resolution strategies where necessary. One concrete design is to show pending status in the UI until the enrollment service confirms the final state, instead of allowing the UI to assume inventory was decremented immediately. Ensure your business logic is idempotent and capable of compensating actions when conflicts appear. Key takeaway: accept eventual consistency where business correctness permits it and design UX and compensating logic to surface intermediate states safely. Eventual Consistency Explained means accept temporary divergence when it improves availability and latency; design uis and compensations to handle interim states safely.. In practical terms, when and how eventual consistency is acceptable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Eventual Consistency
Definition and trade-offs

Eventual consistency allows replicas to be temporarily out of sync to favor availability and performance. Design for this by surfacing pending states and building idempotent operations.

Example
An enrollment initially marked PENDING and later updated to CONFIRMED after payment processes. UIs should show the pending state until confirmation arrives.
Misconception
Eventual consistency is not a bug; it is a model that requires explicit handling, not avoidance at all costs.
Key Takeaway

Model your UX and compensating logic around eventual consistency so users see correct intent while backend converges.

Design cards
UX Pattern: Pending State
Show an explicit pending indicator until all services confirm final state to avoid user confusion.
Conflict Handling
Define conflict resolution rules and use timestamps or last-writer-wins only when appropriate for the domain.
Idempotency
Design operations to be safely repeatable to handle retries during asynchronous convergence.

screens.title: Saga Pattern for Distributed Transactions
screens.narratorSegment: The Saga pattern solves multi-service business transactions by breaking a global transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each updating a single service's database and publishing an event to trigger the next step. There are two main styles. In choreography, services publish and react to events without a central controller. This can be simple and decentralized but harder to reason about as the number of services grows. In orchestration, a central orchestrator—often implemented with AWS Step Functions—drives the sequence, invokes local transactions, and issues compensating actions on failures. The orchestrator gives visibility and easier management of compensations but introduces a coordination component. A concrete enrollment example: the Enrollment service creates a PENDING record and publishes an event; the Payment service processes payment and publishes success or failure; on success the Enrollment service marks CONFIRMED and notifies the Course service to increment counts. If payment fails, compensating transactions mark enrollment FAILED or trigger refunds. Misconception to avoid: don't try two-phase commit across heterogeneous stores; Sagas with compensations and idempotency are the recommended pattern in microservices. Key takeaway: choose choreography for small event-driven flows and orchestration when you need strong control and visibility.

keyIdea.title: Saga summary
keyIdea.text: Use Sagas to sequence local transactions and compensations. Choreography is decentralized; orchestration centralizes control for visibility and easier compensation management.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Saga Pattern
Two implementations
Choreography
Services publish and consume events to drive next steps. Simpler for small flows, harder to trace for larger ones.
Orchestration
A central orchestrator manages the sequence and compensating actions. Use Step Functions when you need control and visibility.
Key Takeaway

Design your Saga style based on complexity and the need for traceability; always plan compensating transactions and idempotency.

Enrollment Saga — Scenario Card
1) Enrollment service writes PENDING to DynamoDB and emits Enrollment Initiated. 2) Payment service processes payment and emits Payment Succeeded or Payment Failed. 3) On success, Enrollment service sets CONFIRMED and optionally calls Course service API to increment counts. 4) On failure, publish failure event and run compensations like refund or mark FAILED.
Anti-pattern
Two-phase commit across services and heterogeneous datastores — avoid due to blocking and availability problems.
Pro tip
Use correlation IDs to trace Saga progress across services and to troubleshoot compensating actions when they run.

screens.title: Replication and Caching Strategies
screens.narratorSegment: Read-heavy workloads benefit from replication and caching. For relational databases, RDS and Aurora support read replicas to offload read traffic from the primary writer, improving scalability. Aurora also offers global databases for cross-region low-latency reads and disaster recovery. For DynamoDB, Global Tables allow multi-region, multi-active replication so each region can serve local reads and writes. Caching with ElastiCache reduces latency by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Cache-aside is the most common pattern: the application checks the cache first, then the database on miss, and writes back to the cache after a database write. Write-through synchronously updates cache and database together, while write-back defers persistence and increases complexity. Misconceptions include assuming cache always simplifies correctness; caches can expose stale data unless you design invalidation and TTLs carefully. Example: use read replicas for analytics and reporting to keep OLTP primary clean, and ElastiCache for product detail pages to reduce database load. Key takeaway: combine appropriate replication and caching patterns to meet latency and scalability goals while planning for cache invalidation and replica lag. Replication and Caching Strategies means use read replicas and global tables for scalable reads and elasticache with considered invalidation strategies to reduce latency and database load.. In practical terms, offload reads and improve latency with replicas and caches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › Replication & Caching
Patterns and AWS features
RDS / Aurora Read Replicas
Offload read traffic; use replicas for reporting and analytics to protect primary throughput.
DynamoDB Global Tables
Multi-region replication for low-latency reads and multi-active writes.
ElastiCache
Use cache-aside for predictable semantics; choose TTLs and invalidation strategies to avoid stale reads.
Global Databases
Aurora Global Database supports cross-region DB replication for disaster recovery and local reads.
Example: Product Pages
Cache product details in ElastiCache with a cache-aside pattern. Use a read replica for analytical queries like "most viewed" dashboards. When product updates occur, invalidate or update the cache and accept brief replica lag for analytics.
Pitfall
Ignoring TTLs and invalidation leads to stale data in cache and user confusion.
Key Takeaway

Design caching and replication together. Plan for invalidation, TTLs, and replica lag to maintain correctness and performance.

screens.title: Distributed Transactions — Challenges & Mitigations
screens.narratorSegment: Distributed transactions across independent databases are challenging because ACID guarantees do not extend across service boundaries. Two-phase commit is often avoided in microservices because it blocks participants and couples availability to all involved systems. Instead, teams use Sagas, compensating transactions, idempotency, correlation IDs, and improved observability to maintain practical correctness. Compensating transactions are explicit steps to undo partial work when a later step fails, such as releasing reserved inventory after a payment failure. Idempotency makes retries safe by ensuring repeated requests produce the same effect as a single request. Correlation IDs let you trace a multi-step business flow across services for debugging and monitoring. Observability, including structured logs and distributed tracing, helps you understand state when compensations run. A misconception is to rely purely on retries without idempotency; retries without guarantees can cause duplicates or incorrect state. Key takeaway: avoid two-phase commit across heterogeneous systems and design for retriable operations, compensations, and traceability so you can operate distributed transactions reliably. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

  • Retries without idempotency cause duplicates or inconsistent state.
Key Takeaway

Design compensating transactions, idempotency, and tracing instead of attempting 2PC across services.

Mitigations
Compensating Transactions
Define actions that undo a previous step when later steps fail, like releasing reservations or issuing refunds.
Idempotency
Design operations to be safe to repeat; use unique request identifiers and conditional writes where available.
Correlation IDs & Observability
Pass a unique ID through all services and use logs/tracing to reconstruct Saga state for troubleshooting.

Module 9 › Chapter 9.5 › DynamoDB Example
Starter Python (Boto3)
import boto3
import json
from botocore.exceptions import ClientError

# Initialize DynamoDB client
dynamodb = boto3.resource('dynamodb', region_name='us-east-1')
table_name = 'Enrollments' # Replace with your DynamoDB table name

def create_enrollment_table():
  try:
    table = dynamodb.create_table(
      TableName=table_name,
      KeySchema=[
        {'AttributeName': 'enrollmentId', 'KeyType': 'HASH'}
      ],
      AttributeDefinitions=[
        {'AttributeName': 'enrollmentId', 'AttributeType': 'S'}
      ],
      ProvisionedThroughput={
        'ReadCapacityUnits': 5,
        'WriteCapacityUnits': 5
      }
    )
    table.wait_until_exists()
    print(f"Table {table_name} created successfully.")
  except ClientError as e:
    if e.response['Error']['Code'] == 'ResourceInUseException':
      print(f"Table {table_name} already exists.")
    else:
      raise e

# Other functions: create_enrollment, update_enrollment_status, get_enrollment
# See chapter content for full examples and recommended safety checks.
Notes
  • Use unique enrollment IDs to ensure idempotent writes when retrying.
  • Publish events after local writes to participate in Sagas.
  • Add conditional writes to prevent races and to make compensations predictable.

screens.title: Security and Access Control for Service Datastores
screens.narratorSegment: Security and access control are essential whenever multiple services and teams manage data. Always encrypt data at rest and in transit for all database services. Use IAM roles and resource-level permissions to ensure each microservice has only the permissions it needs. For example, grant the Enrollment service permissions limited to its table and avoid broad account-level database permissions. A common mistake is using long-lived credentials or embedding access keys in code. Instead, rely on short-lived credentials and instance or task roles. Also, apply network controls such as VPC endpoints or private subnets to limit exposure. When using caches, ensure they are not publicly accessible and that sensitive data stored in memory respects compliance rules. Finally, log and monitor access to databases and use tracing to detect anomalies. Key takeaway: security is not an afterthought — choose encryption, minimal IAM permissions, and network controls before deploying service datastores in production. screens.title: Common Mistakes and Practical Recommendations
screens.narratorSegment: Architects often repeat the same mistakes when migrating to microservices. The most common is leaving a shared database and assuming it preserves simplicity; in reality shared schemas create tight coupling, deployment friction, and blast radius. Another mistake is attempting two-phase commit across heterogeneous databases — it increases blocking and is brittle. Instead, favor Sagas and compensations. Also, teams frequently underestimate the need for observability: without correlation IDs, distributed tracing, and structured logs, debugging cross-service failures is slow and error-prone. Practical recommendations include: design for idempotency so retries are safe; add correlation IDs to every message and A P I call for traceability; plan compensating transactions and make them testable; and apply caching and replication intentionally with invalidation strategy. Finally, secure every datastore with encryption, least-privilege IAM, and VPC controls. Reflect on your architecture: where might you be tempted to centralize data for convenience, and how will you replace that convenience with explicit contracts and event-driven sharing? fullNarratorScript:
In this chapter we explore how data management changes when you move from a single monolithic database to an ecosystem of small, independently deployable services. You will learn why each microservice should own its data store, how polyglot persistence lets you pick the best database type for each service, and how to design for consistency when updates span services. We’ll cover concrete AWS options — managed relational databases for transactional workloads, DynamoDB for high-scale key-value workloads, caches for low-latency reads, graph stores for relationship-rich data, and time-series engines for sensor or metric streams. You will see patterns for consistency such as eventual consistency and the Saga pattern, and practical mitigations like compensating transactions, idempotency, and correlation IDs to trace and debug cross-service flows. A short enrollment example ties these ideas together: an enrollment service using DynamoDB, a course catalog in RDS, and a payments service in RDS that coordinate via events. By the end, you should be able to choose appropriate AWS services, design a Saga for a multi-step business transaction, and apply caching and replication to improve performance while avoiding common mistakes like sharing a single database across services. Consider how your current systems would change if each team owned its own datastore: what constraints and freedoms would that create?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to explain polyglot persistence and why database-per-service supports independent evolution. You will learn to map data access patterns and consistency needs to AWS services such as Aurora, DynamoDB, ElastiCache, Neptune, and Timestream. You will design strategies for cross-service consistency using eventual consistency and the Saga pattern, and decide when choreography or orchestration is more appropriate. You will implement replication and caching patterns to improve read performance and resilience, and understand the limitations of distributed transactions so you can avoid two-phase commit and instead apply compensating transactions, idempotent operations, correlation IDs, and observability. Each objective links a practical skill to why it matters in production systems and includes a short mnemonic to help you remember the milestone. These skills are essential for operating resilient multi-service systems on AWS and for making informed trade-offs between consistency, latency, and availability.

These objectives are practical. You will not only name the services but select the datastore for a real microservice based on access patterns, latency, and consistency expectations. For example, you will decide when a payments service needs a relational store for ACID guarantees versus an enrollment service using DynamoDB for high write throughput. You will design a Saga to coordinate a multi-step workflow, choose choreography for lightweight event-driven flows or Step Functions for orchestration when visibility and control are required. You will also implement caching strategies to reduce read pressure and apply read replicas or global tables for global reads and disaster recovery. Assessment milestones will test your ability to choose services, design compensation for failed steps, and implement idempotent operations. These outcomes ensure you can translate architecture trade-offs into stable, maintainable systems on AWS.

Database per service is a simple but powerful idea: every microservice owns its data and exposes it only through its A P I. This ownership reduces coupling between services because schema changes, migrations, and performance tuning belong to the single responsible team. A concrete example: an Order service owns orders and transactional logic in a relational store, while a Recommendation service owns a graph or document store. A common misconception is assuming a shared database simplifies coordination. While sharing can make joins across domains easy, it creates a tight coupling that prevents independent deployment, can introduce contention, and makes ownership unclear. In practice, ownership encourages clear A P I contracts and forces teams to design explicit data exchange patterns, usually through events or service APIs. The downside is that joins across services are no longer immediate; you design denormalization, A P I composition, or asynchronous synchronization instead. Key takeaway: embrace ownership to reduce blast radius, but plan for how data will be shared via events or well-defined A P I calls. Question to reflect on: which entities in your system benefit most from independent ownership and why?

Choosing the right AWS datastore should start from the access pattern and consistency requirements. Amazon RDS and Aurora are suited for workloads needing strong transactional consistency, complex joins, and ACID semantics — for example, a payments ledger or order management. DynamoDB is ideal when you need massive scale, low-latency key-value or document access such as user sessions or a high-write enrollment log. ElastiCache (Redis or Memcached) is a purpose-built cache for frequently read, mutable data where in-memory latency matters more than durable storage, such as session stores or product detail caching. Neptune fits workloads where relationships are first-class, like recommendations or fraud detection. DocumentDB is useful for flexible schema document models compatible with MongoDB patterns. Timestream is optimized for time-series use cases like IoT sensor streams or application metrics. A frequent error is selecting a relational database for every workload by habit. Instead, base your choice on query patterns, required latency, expected scale, and consistency needs. Example: an Enrollment service that must accept high-volume writes with occasional reads is a good DynamoDB candidate, while the Course catalog with complex joins and normalized relations fits Aurora. Consider replication and cache strategies as part of your datastore decision, not an afterthought. Which trade-offs are acceptable for your service: eventual consistency or immediate transactional guarantees?

Eventual consistency means that if no new updates occur, all replicas of a data item will converge to the latest value over time. This model contrasts with strong consistency, where every read reflects the latest write immediately. Eventual consistency is acceptable for many user experiences where a slight delay is tolerable — for instance, updating a user profile photo across services or reflecting an enrollment status that moves from PENDING to CONFIRMED. A misconception is that eventual consistency is unreliable; in reality, it is a deliberate trade-off to gain availability and latency. Design patterns that embrace eventual consistency include optimistic updates, user-facing pending states, and conflict resolution strategies where necessary. One concrete design is to show pending status in the UI until the enrollment service confirms the final state, instead of allowing the UI to assume inventory was decremented immediately. Ensure your business logic is idempotent and capable of compensating actions when conflicts appear. Key takeaway: accept eventual consistency where business correctness permits it and design UX and compensating logic to surface intermediate states safely. Eventual Consistency Explained means accept temporary divergence when it improves availability and latency; design uis and compensations to handle interim states safely.. In practical terms, when and how eventual consistency is acceptable. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

The Saga pattern solves multi-service business transactions by breaking a global transaction into a sequence of local transactions, each updating a single service's database and publishing an event to trigger the next step. There are two main styles. In choreography, services publish and react to events without a central controller. This can be simple and decentralized but harder to reason about as the number of services grows. In orchestration, a central orchestrator—often implemented with AWS Step Functions—drives the sequence, invokes local transactions, and issues compensating actions on failures. The orchestrator gives visibility and easier management of compensations but introduces a coordination component. A concrete enrollment example: the Enrollment service creates a PENDING record and publishes an event; the Payment service processes payment and publishes success or failure; on success the Enrollment service marks CONFIRMED and notifies the Course service to increment counts. If payment fails, compensating transactions mark enrollment FAILED or trigger refunds. Misconception to avoid: don't try two-phase commit across heterogeneous stores; Sagas with compensations and idempotency are the recommended pattern in microservices. Key takeaway: choose choreography for small event-driven flows and orchestration when you need strong control and visibility.

Read-heavy workloads benefit from replication and caching. For relational databases, RDS and Aurora support read replicas to offload read traffic from the primary writer, improving scalability. Aurora also offers global databases for cross-region low-latency reads and disaster recovery. For DynamoDB, Global Tables allow multi-region, multi-active replication so each region can serve local reads and writes. Caching with ElastiCache reduces latency by storing frequently accessed data in memory. Cache-aside is the most common pattern: the application checks the cache first, then the database on miss, and writes back to the cache after a database write. Write-through synchronously updates cache and database together, while write-back defers persistence and increases complexity. Misconceptions include assuming cache always simplifies correctness; caches can expose stale data unless you design invalidation and TTLs carefully. Example: use read replicas for analytics and reporting to keep OLTP primary clean, and ElastiCache for product detail pages to reduce database load. Key takeaway: combine appropriate replication and caching patterns to meet latency and scalability goals while planning for cache invalidation and replica lag. Replication and Caching Strategies means use read replicas and global tables for scalable reads and elasticache with considered invalidation strategies to reduce latency and database load.. In practical terms, offload reads and improve latency with replicas and caches. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Distributed transactions across independent databases are challenging because ACID guarantees do not extend across service boundaries. Two-phase commit is often avoided in microservices because it blocks participants and couples availability to all involved systems. Instead, teams use Sagas, compensating transactions, idempotency, correlation IDs, and improved observability to maintain practical correctness. Compensating transactions are explicit steps to undo partial work when a later step fails, such as releasing reserved inventory after a payment failure. Idempotency makes retries safe by ensuring repeated requests produce the same effect as a single request. Correlation IDs let you trace a multi-step business flow across services for debugging and monitoring. Security and access control are essential whenever multiple services and teams manage data. Always encrypt data at rest and in transit for all database services. Use IAM roles and resource-level permissions to ensure each microservice has only the permissions it needs. For example, grant the Enrollment service permissions limited to its table and avoid broad account-level database permissions. A common mistake is using long-lived credentials or embedding access keys in code. Instead, rely on short-lived credentials and instance or task roles. When using caches, ensure they are not publicly accessible and that sensitive data stored in memory respects compliance rules. Architects often repeat the same mistakes when migrating to microservices. The most common is leaving a shared database and assuming it preserves simplicity; in reality shared schemas create tight coupling, deployment friction, and blast radius. Another mistake is attempting two-phase commit across heterogeneous databases — it increases blocking and is brittle. Instead, favor Sagas and compensations. Also, teams frequently underestimate the need for observability: without correlation IDs, distributed tracing, and structured logs, debugging cross-service failures is slow and error-prone. Practical recommendations include: design for idempotency so retries are safe; add correlation IDs to every message and A P I call for traceability; plan compensating transactions and make them testable; and apply caching and replication intentionally with invalidation strategy. Finally, secure every datastore with encryption, least-privilege IAM, and VPC controls. Reflect on your architecture: where might you be tempted to centralize data for convenience, and how will you replace that convenience with explicit contracts and event-driven sharing? These three cards summarize the most important ideas from this chapter. First, data ownership and database-per-service reduce coupling and let teams evolve independently. Second, polyglot persistence means choosing the datastore that fits access patterns — Aurora for transactional integrity, DynamoDB for scale, ElastiCache for low-latency reads, and specialized engines for graph or time-series needs. Third, maintain consistency across services using eventual consistency and Sagas with compensations, idempotency, and correlation IDs rather than trying to force two-phase commit across heterogeneous systems.
